I want to go home now.
I want to learn more Korean.
I want to meet a friend.

Where do you want to go?

-아/어 보이다 means 'looks ...' and attaches to the 아/어 form of an adjective.
You look young in that outfit.
Your face looks tired.
This food looks spicy.
The child looks very healthy.
That bag looks expensive.
You look busy today.
My older brother looks angry.
My younger sibling looks sad.
That problem looks easy.
This room looks big.
That person looks old.
This bread looks soft.
The road is wet, so it seems it rained.
-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다 means 'it seems that ...' based on evidence; use -는 for present verbs, -(으)ㄴ for past or adjectives, -(으)ㄹ for future.
My friend did not come to school, so he/she seems to be sick.
The child is crying, so he/she seems to be hungry.
There are many people, so it seems to be a popular restaurant.
After a noun, 모양이다 needs the copula in its adnominal form (-인).
He is holding an umbrella, so it seems it will rain.
That person seems to be Korean.
His bag is gone, so it seems he has already gone home.
My friend is smiling, so he/she seems to be in a good mood.
The room is quiet, so it seems nobody is there.
His face is gloomy, so it seems he did poorly on the test.
Those new sneakers look comfortable, so I want to buy a pair too.
-아/어 보이다 describes how something looks from its appearance (the adjective takes the -아/어 form, then 보이다). -는 모양이다 is a guess based on evidence you can see, often after '-는 걸 보니'.
That restaurant's door is closed, so it seems to be closed today.
This outfit looks more elegant in person than in the photo.
The children are gathering on the field, so a game seems about to begin.
My younger sibling looks much smarter with glasses on.
A: A teammate looks tired these days. B: Right. They seem to have worked until late last night, too. A: Then shall we buy lunch today? B: Good idea. Let's buy coffee for them as well.
I like delicious food.
An adjective before a noun takes -(으)ㄴ (after a consonant) or -ㄴ (after a vowel); 있다/없다 words take -는.
I bought pretty flowers.
I need a small bag.
I want to live in a big house.
I have a good friend.
The person reading a book over there is my younger sibling.
A verb before a noun takes -는 for present, -(으)ㄴ for past and -(으)ㄹ for a future or intended action.
The food I ate yesterday was delicious.
The movie I saw yesterday was fun.
The friend I will meet tomorrow is a student.
I bought clothes to wear tomorrow.
On days when it rains, I stay home.
I have a friend who lives in Korea.
ㅂ-irregular adjectives change ㅂ to 우 before -ㄴ, and ㄹ-verbs drop ㄹ before -는.
The person over there is the teacher.
There are many people who have no money.
I like tall people.
The person smiling in the photo is my mother.
The bag I bought yesterday is expensive.
The food I like is bulgogi.
Who is the person you met yesterday?
I dislike hot weather.
This is a difficult problem.
pretty clothes

An adnominal ending goes on the verb or adjective before a noun: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는 (or -ㄴ/은 for adjectives), future/intended -(으)ㄹ, and -던 for a past habit or an unfinished past action. The tense depends on when the described action happens, not on the main verb.
I often listen to songs that are popular these days.
The house I will move to next month is close to the school.
I want to study in a cafe that is not noisy.
A colleague I used to work with last year called yesterday.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
-아/어서 links a reason or a sequence (do A, then B); it cannot be used with requests, and its tense is shown only at the end.
It rained, so I stayed home.
I went to school and met a friend.
This outfit is pretty but expensive.
-지만 means 'but' and attaches to the plain stem of verbs, adjectives and 이다.
Korean is difficult but fun.
It is cold, so please close the door.
-(으)면 means 'if/when', while -(으)니까 gives a reason that can lead to a request or discovery.
When I opened the door, there was a cat.
If you have time, let's watch a movie together.
If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home.
I study Korean in order to go to Korea.
-(으)려고 + verb states a purpose ('in order to'), and -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 sets a background or a mild contrast.
I went to the bookstore to buy a book.
I took the subway to meet a friend.
I live in Seoul, but my friend lives in Busan.
The food is delicious, but it is too expensive.
It is raining, and I have no umbrella.
I eat a meal and then drink coffee.
-고 lists actions or qualities in order ('and').
My older sister is tall and pretty.
On the weekend I watched a movie and also went shopping.
I had no money, so I couldn't buy it.
I had a headache, so I went to the hospital.
I have a lot of work, but I will leave early today.
I don't know Korean, so it is hard.
If I drink coffee, I can't fall asleep.
I went to the library in order to study.
I washed my hair before meeting my friend.
Time connectors attach to the verb stem in a fixed form: -기 전에 (before), -(으)ㄴ 후에 (after), -(으)ㄹ 때 (when), -자마자 (as soon as). -(으)러 means 'in order to' only with 가다/오다 and similar verbs of movement.
I play games after I finish my homework.
Please don't look at your phone when you cross the street.
I was thirsty, so I went to get some water.
I took a shower as soon as I got home.
A: What happened this morning? B: The bus broke down, so I switched to the subway. A: That must have been hard. B: Not really. I still got here before the meeting started.

Formal polite statements end in -ㅂ니다 after a vowel and -습니다 after a consonant; questions use -ㅂ니까 / -습니까.
What is your name?
I eat a meal.
I drink coffee.
I go to school.
I am at home now.
It is raining now.
The weather is very good today.
I am very busy today.
I watched a movie yesterday.
The formal past is -았/었습니다 and the formal future is -(으)ㄹ 겁니다; questions swap 다 for 까.
I will meet a friend tomorrow.
What did you do on the weekend?
Where are you now?
This book is interesting.
Verbs ending in ㄹ drop it before ㅂ, so the formal form has no ㄹ before -ㅂ니다.
I open the shop door in the morning.
Are you Korean?
I get up at seven in the morning.
My younger sibling is tall.
do (you) eat? (formal)
The meeting starts at two in the afternoon.

The formal polite endings -ㅂ니다/-습니다 (statements) and -ㅂ니까/-습니까 (questions) are used at work, in announcements and with customers. Honorific -(으)시- is added only for the person being respected, not for things or events.
The guest has just arrived.
Where can I get the application form?
We will apply the new rules starting next week.
Our company is near City Hall in Seoul.
A: Hello. Please tell me the name the reservation is under. B: It is Kim Minsu. The reservation is for three people. A: Yes, I have confirmed it. I will show you to a table by the window.
I can swim.
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 means 'can' (ability or possibility) and -(으)ㄹ 수 없다 means 'cannot'.
I can talk in Korean.
I am busy today, so I cannot go.
I cannot eat spicy food.
Can you come tomorrow?
This problem is hard, so I cannot solve it.
I have to get up early tomorrow.
-아/어야 하다 (or 되다) means 'must / have to' and attaches to the 아/어 form of the verb.
I have to do my homework today.
I caught a cold, so I have to take medicine.
I have to go now.
I have to study Korean hard.
May I take a photo here?
-아/어도 되다 asks or gives permission ('may / it is OK to'); a negative before it means 'don't have to'.
You may read this book.
Is it OK to eat now?
You don't have to come early tomorrow.
I have been to Korea.
-(으)ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 says whether you have ever done something; 아/어 보다 often comes before it.
I have never made kimchi.
Have you ever worn a hanbok?
I have never been to Jeju.
I have ridden on an airplane.
I have never met a Korean friend.
Have you ever seen that movie?
You can do it!

No, you can't do that.

-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다 means knowing or not knowing how to do something. -(으)면 안 되다 is a prohibition and -(으)면 되다 means 'it is enough to'. -(으)ㄹ까요 with -아/어도 asks whether something is allowed. 못 or -지 못하다 expresses inability.
You must not talk loudly in the library.
You just have to press this button.
Would it be all right if I sat here for a moment?
My hand hurts, so I can't write.
The plain present of a verb is stem + ㄴ다 after a vowel or 는다 after a consonant; adjectives and 있다/없다 just add 다.
My younger sibling reads a book.
My friend is eating now.
It rained yesterday.
The plain past is -았/었다, the plain future is -(으)ㄹ 것이다, and nouns take -(이)다.
This is my book.
Tomorrow is Saturday.
Yesterday was Sunday.
The weather is good today.
This food is delicious.
The weather was cold yesterday.
The baby is sleeping now.
My older brother rests at home.
We live in Seoul.
Verbs ending in ㄹ drop it before ㄴ and add ㄴ다.
He opens the door.
There are students in the classroom.
That movie was boring.
Where are you going now?
Casual plain questions end in -니 or -냐; they attach to the stem and make the past with -았/었니.
Did you eat?
What did you do yesterday?
Is that person a student?
Who is coming?

Today is Sunday.

I couldn't eat because I was studying.
-느라고 attaches to a verb stem and gives the cause of a (usually negative) result; both clauses share the same subject.
I couldn't sleep because I was doing my homework.
I missed the call because I was talking with a friend.
I was exhausted from cleaning.
I was busy cooking.
I didn't do my homework because I was playing games.
I didn't hear the ring because I was listening to music.
I woke up late because I was reading until late.
I couldn't watch the movie because I was taking photos.

I am busy these days because I am preparing for the exam.
Even though it is snowing, there are many people.
-는데도 / -(으)ㄴ데도 means 'even though'; use -는데도 after verbs and 있다/없다, and -(으)ㄴ데도 after adjectives.
Even though I studied hard, I did badly on the test.
Past tense goes before -는데도 (-았/었는데도), never before -느라고.
Even though I ate a lot, I am hungry.
Even though it is cold, I exercise outside.
Even though I took medicine, my head hurts.
Even though I had no money, I bought expensive clothes.
Even though I practice often, Korean is hard.
Even though the teacher explained, I still don't understand well.
Even though the price is high, there are many people.

Even though it is night, it is bright outside.
Even though I got up early, I was late.
Even though he/she is short, he/she is good at basketball.
I couldn't go to club meetings often because I was working part-time.
Even when the road is congested, the bus always arrives on time.
I forgot to even eat lunch because I was writing a report.

Although our house is small, friends often come to visit.
Because I was helping a coworker, I couldn't finish my own work by closing time.
My friend asked if I have time tomorrow.
Reported questions use -냐고 (verbs, adjectives, 있다/없다, past -았/었냐고) and (이)냐고 for nouns, followed by 묻다 or 하다.
The teacher asked where I am going.
My younger sibling asked what we are eating for dinner.
Mom asked if I had eaten.
My friend asked if this bag is expensive.
The child asked what this is.
Someone asked if that person is a student.
My friend asked what I did on the weekend.
My older sister asked if it will rain tomorrow.
The future is reported with -(으)ㄹ 거냐고; ㄹ-verbs drop the ㄹ before 냐고.
The teacher asked if Korean is difficult.
A friend asked where I live.
Dad asked what time I am coming.
A friend asked if I had seen the movie.
The clerk asked how many people there were.
My younger sibling asked when I went to Korea.

A friend asked if the weather was cold.
Mom is asking whether I finished all my homework.
What did you say?
You did not catch what the other person just said and ask them to repeat it.
The teacher told us to be quiet.
A reported command is -(으)라고 하다 (-으라고 after a consonant, -라고 after a vowel or ㄹ); a reported suggestion is -자고 하다.
Mom told me to go to bed early.
A friend suggested watching a movie together.
The doctor told me to take the medicine.
Dad told me to close the door.
A friend suggested hanging out on the weekend.
My younger sibling suggested we eat lunch together.
A friend suggested meeting early tomorrow.
Mom told me to do my homework first.
A friend told me to call him/her.
My older sister told me to wait here.
The teacher told us to speak in Korean.
A friend told me to come to his/her house.
The doctor told me not to drink alcohol.
Negative reported commands use -지 말라고 and negative suggestions use -지 말자고.
A friend suggested that we not go there.
The teacher told me to open the window.
Verbs ending in ㄹ take -라고, not -으라고, in reported commands.
A friend suggested taking a photo together.
Mom told me to take an umbrella.
A friend suggested studying together because there is a test tomorrow.
Dad told me to get up quickly.
The teacher told us to look at the board.

A statement is reported with -ㄴ/는다고 하다 for verbs, plain -다고 for adjectives and 있다/없다, and (이)라고 for nouns.
My friend says Korean is difficult.
My younger sibling said he/she was hungry.
The teacher said there is a test tomorrow.
Mom said it will rain this evening.
For past or future events use -았/었다고 and -(으)ㄹ 거라고 before 하다.
Dad says he is driving now.
They say that person is a doctor.
He says he is my friend's older brother.

My younger sibling says he/she watched a movie yesterday.
My friend says he/she is eating now.
My older sister says she exercises every day.
The news said it will snow tomorrow.
My friend said Korean food is delicious.
My younger sibling said he/she has no homework.
My boyfriend says he is busy these days.
My friend said he/she is not going to school today.
My younger sibling said he/she is hanging out at home.
ㄹ-verbs drop the ㄹ before ㄴ when forming the plain present.
My friend says he/she lives in Seoul.
My friend said the room is cold.

I said I was fine.

B: He said he can't come today because he caught a cold.
My younger sibling pretends to be sick.
-는 척하다 means 'pretend to (do)' for present verbs and 있다/없다; use -(으)ㄴ 척하다 after adjectives and 이다.
My friend pretended to have finished all the homework.
To pretend to have done something already, use the past -(으)ㄴ 척하다 on a verb.
That person pretends to be rich.
I pretended not to see the teacher.
I acted like I was fine, but actually I was sad.
My friend pretends to be good at Korean.
My younger sibling pretends to study and plays games.
That student pretended to understand what the teacher said.
The child pretended not to cry.
Negatives work inside the pretense: 안 + verb or -지 않다 become 안 V는 척 or V지 않는 척.
My friend pretended not to hear the phone call.
My younger sibling pretended not to be angry.
That person pretends to be kind, but actually isn't.
My younger sibling pretends to be a grown-up.
The child pretended not to be sick.
My older brother acts as if nothing happened.
I pretended to have taken the medicine.
My friend pretended to have paid.
I pretended to smile, but I felt bad inside.
My younger sibling only pretends to clean and then plays.
My friend pretended to have been to Korea.
My younger sibling pretended to have gotten up early.
The more I study Korean, the more fun it is.
-(으)ㄹ수록 means 'the more ... the more ...'; it attaches to verb and adjective stems, and ㄹ-stems take -수록 directly.
The more I eat these snacks, the more I want to eat.
The older you get, the faster time goes.
The more you talk with a friend, the closer you become.
The higher you go, the colder it is.
The cheaper the price, the better.
The farther the distance, the higher the taxi fare.
The harder it gets, the harder you have to work.
ㅂ- and ㄷ-irregular stems change their final sound before -(으)ㄹ수록.
The colder the weather, the tastier warm tea is.
The more you listen, the better the song is.
The more I use it, the more comfortable it gets.
The more I practice, the better I get.
The earlier you go, the better.
The bigger it is, the more expensive it is.
If you work hard, good results are bound to follow.
-기 마련이다 says something is bound to happen or is only natural; it attaches to a plain stem.
After winter passes, spring is bound to come.
At first, it is natural for everyone to find it hard.
Things are bound to break down if you use them for a long time.
Children are bound to grow up quickly.
When it rains, the roads are bound to be jammed.
If you go to bed late, you are bound to be tired.
Everything is bound to have an end.
Money is bound to disappear when you spend it.
I should have brought an umbrella.
Verb stem + -(으)ㄹ 걸 그랬어요 expresses regret about something you did not do ('I should have ...').
I should have gone to bed early yesterday.

I should have called my friend.
I should have taken a taxi.
I should have eaten more.
I should have gone to the party yesterday.
I should have done the homework in advance.
I should have taken photos.
I should have read that book.
I should have eaten breakfast before coming.
I should have worn warm clothes.
I should have invited my friend.
I should have walked.
I shouldn't have bought it.
Use -지 말 걸 그랬어요 to say 'I shouldn't have ...' about something you did.
I shouldn't have stayed out playing so late yesterday.
I shouldn't have told a lie.
I should have left early.
I should have stayed home.
I should have drunk more water.
I should have asked for directions.
I should have learned more English.
I should have gotten up earlier.
I should have given my friend a present.
I should have charged my phone beforehand.
-(으)ㄹ 걸 그랬어요 expresses regret about something you did not do. For something you did that you now regret, use -지 말 걸 그랬어요. The verb before 걸 is always in the -(으)ㄹ form.
If I had known the road would be jammed, I should have taken the subway.
I should have reviewed once more before the exam.
I shouldn't have gotten so angry.
I should have heard my friend out.

Verbs can take a short causative suffix (i, hi, ri, gi, or u) to mean making someone do an action; the suffix is fixed for each verb.
to empty

Some adjective and intransitive stems also form causatives that mean making something become that state.
to leave behind, to leave over
to make (someone) go hungry
to deceive, to trick
to turn, to spin
The baby is sleepy, so the mother puts the baby to sleep.
A causative verb is transitive, so the person made to act is usually marked with the object particle or a dative particle.

That comedian always makes people laugh.

The mother puts shoes on the child.

We keep and raise a puppy at our house.

I parked the car in the parking lot.
I boiled ramen and ate it.

I hid the present in the drawer.

The company doubled its office space.
A report that identified the cause of the accident was released today.
If you show the customer a sample first, the chance of a contract goes up.
to make (someone) study
The causative pattern makes or lets someone do something; the person made to act is marked with the object particle or a dative particle.
to make (someone) sit
to make (something) clean
An adjective plus the causative pattern means making something or someone become that state.
to let (someone) come in
to make (something) bright
to make (someone) say something

formal statement ending after a consonant
Formal statements use one ending after a vowel or the letter l-final stem and another after a consonant; l-stem verbs drop the final l.
formal question ending after a consonant

formal polite command ending

formal ending for 'I will' or intention

Thank you for using our service.

Report on the customer satisfaction survey. This year's satisfaction was 78 points, 4 points higher than last year's 74. Review opinion on the results of the local small business support program. The average monthly sales of the thirty supported businesses rose 18 percent compared with before the program began. Report on road safety in the jurisdiction. This year's traffic accidents numbered 1,200, up 6 percent from last year, but the number of registered vehicles in the same period rose 11 percent. According to a research institute's report, over the last five years a tendency appeared for the juvenile crime rate to fall in cities and counties where libraries increased. This is because regions with ample finances increased not only libraries but also after-school programs. The institute added that to confirm the independent effect of library expansion, regions with similar fiscal conditions must be compared with one another.

The results of the citizen opinion survey are summarized. For the project in question, support was 62 percent, opposition 31 percent, and no response 7 percent. However, the response rate was only 4 percent, and respondents aged 65 or older, at 52 percent, greatly exceeded their actual population share of 24 percent. The research team also presented figures adjusted so that age shares match the actual population composition; after adjustment, support fell to 54 percent but was still higher than opposition. The team stated that the direction of support being ahead is maintained, but that the gap should be interpreted as smaller than the original figures.

Third-quarter operating results report. Net income was 12 billion won, up about 35 percent from the same period last year. However, 2.5 billion won of this is a one-time gain from selling an idle plot of land. Excluding it, the growth rate of net income stays in single digits. Moreover, operating profit, which shows the profit from the core business of selling products, fell 2 percent. The finance team judges that reading the rise in net income as a sign the business is improving is premature. This assessment will be revisited after checking whether the same structure repeats next quarter.

Monthly housing market trends report. This month's apartment transaction volume in the capital region rose 3 percent from the previous month, but looking at the last three months' flow it is effectively in a sideways phase. The price index also rose only 0.2 percent, which can be seen as a change within the margin of error. Meanwhile, there are reports from the brokerage industry that inquiries rose after the loan interest rate cut, but this has not yet been confirmed in transaction statistics. Therefore the report takes the position that it is too early to judge that the market has entered a recovery phase.

A research institute surveyed 1,200 office workers: respondents who work from home at least twice a week reported an average job satisfaction of 78 points, higher than the 65 of office-based workers. On this basis the institute announced that remote work raises productivity. But the survey asked only for self-rated satisfaction and did not measure actual performance. Moreover, remote-work participants are mostly concentrated in jobs with a lot of autonomy, so it is hard to tell whether the satisfaction gap comes from the way of working or from the nature of the jobs. Therefore these results alone are insufficient to draw the conclusion that remote work raises productivity.

The ratio of housing costs to income across all households averages 22 percent, the same level as five years ago. Some take this as grounds to say that the housing burden has not changed. However, the ratio for the lowest-income 20 percent of households rose from 31 to 38 percent, while that of the top 20 percent fell from 15 to 12 percent. The rise on one side and the fall on the other canceled each other out, and the average merely stayed the same. An average tells us the center of the whole but does not show the changes that took place between groups. Therefore one must not leap from the fact that the average is the same to the conclusion that every household's burden is the same.

In its first year, the newly opened Hansol Library had 40 percent more visitors than the previous year, and the city judged that citizens' reading culture had spread. Yet in the same period, books borrowed rose by only 3 percent. In a user survey, a majority said they came to study in the reading room. The number of visitors may be an indicator reflecting a facility's accessibility and comfort, but it does not directly represent the amount of reading. To speak of the spread of reading culture, other indicators such as the number of books borrowed or reading time must be presented together.

This year's consumer price inflation was officially 2.1 percent, but many citizens feel that living costs rose much more than that. Over this gap, criticism arises that the statistics distort reality. However, a price index is a value calculated by setting item weights according to the spending structure of an average household. In a year when food prices rise 5 percent, the rate felt by low-income households that spend a lot on food is bound to be higher than the average. In the end, the gap between the official figure and what people feel arises not because the calculation is wrong but because one number cannot represent every household.

Sales of a new beverage rose 20 percent in the three months after advertising began in June compared with the previous three months. The marketing team presented this graph as evidence of the advertising effect. However, this drink is a product whose demand rises in summer, and even last year, with no advertising, sales rose 18 percent over the same period. Taking this into account, the increase attributable to advertising is at most around 2 percentage points. Still, the weather and competing products may have differed between last year and this year, so even this figure is hard to regard as a confirmed effect.

When an online shopping mall ran a customer satisfaction survey, 35 percent of respondents chose 'very dissatisfied.' Some executives thought a serious problem had arisen in the service. But the survey's response rate was only 12 percent, and customers with complaints tend to respond to surveys more actively. Therefore the 35 percent figure cannot be read as the evaluation of all customers. That does not mean this data is useless, however. The reasons for dissatisfaction that respondents wrote down can be clues indicating which areas should be improved first.

The average score of students who skip breakfast was 6 points lower than that of students who eat it. This result is often cited as grounds for the claim that eating breakfast raises academic achievement. But when only students from households with similar incomes were compared, the score gap shrank to 1.5 points. This is because students from lower-income families are more likely to skip breakfast and often also have disadvantaged study environments. This analysis does not mean that breakfast has no effect at all, but it clearly shows that a considerable part of the initially observed gap is explained by other factors.

Today we will look at the preservation of hanok from the viewpoint of cultural heritage policy. A hanok is not merely a living space but a cultural product in which climate and way of life are condensed. The topic of today's lecture is how to handle cultural context in translation. Literal translation has the advantage of being faithful to the original, but it can leave meanings that feel strange to readers. Conversely, free translation is easy to read, but there is a risk that the character of the original is erased. We will compare the strengths and weaknesses of the two approaches with examples.

A: There is much debate about the custom of asking age first when people meet. How do you see it? B: Since Korean changes forms of address and speech style depending on the other person, I see asking age as a practical procedure for setting the frame of the conversation. C: I accept that function, but doesn't it result in a structure in which the older side leads the conversation becoming entrenched? B: I do not deny that such a side effect exists. But that is a result the custom produced, not the reason the custom arose. If the system of address changes, the question will naturally decrease too.

A: How can we explain the culture of exchanging holiday gifts and even making sure to return them? B: I see it as a sign of long-term trust. The wish to return what one received becomes a cord that keeps the relationship going. C: But if people try to return exactly what they received, isn't it effectively no different from a transaction? B: On the surface it can look that way. But if it were a transaction, the relationship would end the moment the price is paid. Deliberately adding a little extra to the return gift so that a debt remains means one does not intend to end the relationship. I do not deny that calculation exists. It is just that the purpose of that calculation is continuation, not settling accounts.

A: Some criticize everyday hanbok, adapted so it can be worn in daily life, as damaging tradition. C: I think that if the structure, such as the proportion of jacket and skirt and the use of the ribbon ties, is not kept, it is hard to call it hanbok. B: I agree that the basic structure should be respected. But if we insist on the old form even in material, length, and way of fastening, there may be no one left to wear it. C: You mean that if no one wears it, the tradition is cut off. B: Yes. A garment placed in a museum and a garment people wear are preserved in different ways. I think the latter lasts longer.

A: Households living with their parents have decreased; has awareness of filial piety weakened? B: I think it has not so much weakened as changed its form of expression. Even if people do not live together, filial piety continues by sharing hospital bills and keeping in frequent contact. C: That interpretation presupposes that the family continues to be in charge of care. Isn't that very premise the problem? B: The question itself is valid. But until the system provides sufficient support, that premise cannot be erased overnight. Only after the system is in place can we talk about filial piety as a choice rather than an obligation.

A: The number of households making kimchi themselves is falling. Is the kimchi-making culture disappearing? B: It is hard to judge by the number of households that make it alone. Even if people buy it, if the practice of sharing with neighbors and asking after them remains, the culture continues. C: But if the process of gathering to work together disappears, won't that sharing not last long either? B: That concern has merit. That is why our institute is putting its effort into recording and supporting the practice of gathering and sharing, rather than the taste of kimchi.

A: They say that postponing work start times and even adjusting aircraft takeoffs and landings on exam day looks strange to foreigners. B: I understand it as a social promise to protect the fairness of the exam. It is an effort to let everyone take the test under the same conditions. C: Doesn't that consideration, on the other hand, increase the burden examinees feel? B: It may. But if we withdraw the consideration, inequality of conditions would arise. I think reducing the burden must start not from adjusting the scale of the consideration but from fixing the structure in which there is only one chance to take the exam.

A: In some regions, a system has been created in which people exchange each other's labor, calculated in hours. Can it be called a modern version of pumasi? B: I think it inherits the spirit. It is the same in that effort is repaid with relationships rather than money. C: But as the scale grows, doesn't the cost of recording and managing hours rise and efficiency fall? B: That is a fair point. So I think such a system works best in a small village where people know each other, and expanding it to a whole city is unreasonable. However, I want to add that the value of this system lies in relationships, not efficiency.

It is often said that competition is the driving force of progress. Certainly competition does draw out effort. If so, the problem is not whether competition exists but its degree and form. In the end, what we should ask is not whether to abolish competition but what kind of competition to design.

A: I am in favor of expanding remote work. It shortens commuting time, which raises employees' quality of life. B: I acknowledge the advantage you mention. Some people worry that early English education hinders mother-tongue development. But this worry rests on the premise that a child's chances of encountering the mother tongue are reduced by the foreign language. In reality, quite a few studies show that for children who use their mother tongue amply at home, exposure to a foreign language does not harm native-language ability. The crux is not whether a foreign language is learned early but how well the mother-tongue environment is maintained. If the premise changes, the conclusion must change too.

This report assesses that the citizen-participation budgeting system has raised fiscal transparency. But the only evidence offered is a satisfaction survey of participating citizens. High satisfaction does not necessarily mean that finances have become transparent. Had objective indicators such as the level of disclosure of budget execution or the number of audit findings been presented as well, trust in the conclusion would have been much higher. In the end, the report's conclusion has gone too far ahead of its evidence.

But basing the purpose of the straw regulation only on the amount of waste reduced is a narrow interpretation. This is because the regulation is a symbolic starting point that questions consumption habits that took disposable items for granted. When judging its effect, therefore, we must weigh changes in awareness as well as volume.

But looking back at history, technology eliminated some occupations yet also created occupations that had not existed before. It is too early to be optimistic on this basis. Past transitions unfolded over decades, whereas the present change is much faster. If there is not enough time to adapt, the mere fact that new jobs appear cannot ease individual anxiety.

What this metaphor is trying to say is that an approach changing public transport and urban structure together is needed.

Just because the grounds are sufficient, it cannot necessarily be said that the conclusion is correct.

The biggest advantage of remote work is that it cuts commuting time, because the time once spent commuting can be used for rest and self-development. However, it is hard to deny the limitation that collaboration among members becomes difficult. Therefore, rather than applying the same method to every job, it is desirable to flexibly combine office and remote work according to the nature of the work.

In one survey, students who skip breakfast showed lower grades on average. On this basis, an argument was raised for making breakfast mandatory. However, many of the students who skip breakfast were short of sleep because they attended cram schools until late at night. To sort out which factor affects grades, a comparison with sleep time held to the same conditions is needed. The survey was conducted on two hundred students at three middle schools.

The city is considering closing a municipal swimming pool. The fact that operating costs per user are double those of a nearby private facility was presented as the main grounds. But this figure includes free use by seniors and children, and the medical costs reduced by users' improved health are left out of the calculation. Who set the basis of comparison, and through what procedure, was not made public. The city plans to set its final policy as early as next month. A users' group has started a signature campaign against closure.

The argument that remote medical care should be fully permitted gains particular persuasiveness in regions where medical institutions are sparse. However, the counterargument that, for first-visit patients, the possibility of misdiagnosis is hard to rule out without an in-person examination cannot be taken lightly either. In the end, the point at issue seems to lie less in the either-or of permission versus prohibition than in which care to permit under which conditions. This issue is scheduled to be handled as a main agenda item at a medical system improvement forum to be held within this year.

The saying that compares history to a mirror is common. But a mirror merely reflects what stands before it, and does not itself decide where to reflect and where to cover. In the process by which history is narrated, a choice about what to record and what to leave out is made first. The same event remains as a completely different scene depending on who writes it and in which era. This is because how sources are chosen and arranged is itself the starting point of interpretation. What the mirror metaphor misses is the hand of the one doing the reflecting.

There are many studies showing that tightening speed limits reduces traffic fatalities. However, most of these studies targeted sections where enforcement cameras were also installed. Whether the same result would appear in places without enforcement has not yet been verified. The concern that legislation that merely changes the number on the speed limit may fail to produce the expected results comes from this. This question has been raised repeatedly in regions with differing road environments. Discussion of the related bill is currently stalled.

A: There is a report that average sleep time increased after implementation in a country that legally blocked teenagers' late-night game access. B: That report tracked only one year after the regulation, was limited to students in a single city, and there is also a separate survey showing that circumvention increased. A: The existence of circumvention does not make the regulation meaningless. Even if some circumvent it, connection time itself has decreased. B: I am not saying it is meaningless; I am saying we need to be more careful in stating the size of the effect.

A company advertises that its average employee salary is among the top in the industry. However, this average includes the pay of three executives. The company plans to halve its new-hiring scale this year compared with last year. The labor union claims that if the executives are excluded and the median is calculated, the figure falls short even of the industry average. But the company has not disclosed how it calculated the average, and the union's calculation likewise has not had its data source presented. The promotional phrase was also posted on the internal bulletin board.
It is hard to draw a firm conclusion about the policy's effect from this result alone.
Hedged endings such as -(으)ㄹ 것으로 보이다 and -기 어렵다 keep a formal written claim tentative instead of asserting it outright.
Before deciding whether to introduce the system, an examination of the anticipated side effects must come first.
Nominalised noun phrases ending in -(으)ㄴ/는 + noun, -다는/-리라는 + noun, or -에 대한 + noun compress a whole clause so that it can serve as the subject of a formal sentence.
If this interpretation is valid, it seems that the existing theory will have to be revised.
Since the sample size is not sufficient, this result should be accepted as provisional.
Expectations were raised that, if regulation is eased, the entry of new firms will become active.
The report in question will probably find it hard to escape criticism that it overestimated the policy's results.
This phenomenon is interpreted as the result of several factors acting in combination rather than a single cause.
If the scope of the discussion is widened, there is a concern that the core issue may instead become blurred.

Some researchers argue that applying different minimum wages by region would revive jobs in the provinces. If labor costs fall, small workplaces gain the capacity to hire more, they say. This logic is not entirely baseless. However, if the wage gap widens, young people may leave even more for the capital region, and the local labor force itself may shrink. If there is no one left to work, the added jobs will not be filled either. Therefore, differential application is worth considering only when complementary measures to stop population outflow are prepared at the same time.

Cases keep occurring in which administrative agencies, even after receiving a freedom-of-information request, withhold documents citing the protection of personal information. No one disagrees that protecting personal information is an important value. But hiding wholesale even documents that could be released if only identifying details such as names or addresses were covered is closer to dodging responsibility than to protection. Non-disclosure should be the exception, and when applying the exception, the agency must prove the necessity. In the end, the issue is not whether to disclose or not, but how far one needs to cover.

After a research institute announced survey results showing that students who skip breakfast have lower grades, the claim spread that breakfast raises grades. The survey does confirm that the two variables move together. But for this to count as evidence of causation, the influence of other factors such as family circumstances or sleep time must be ruled out. This survey did not control for such factors. Therefore, what the results show is only a correlation, and it is still insufficient as a basis for a policy recommending breakfast.

The principle that the original form must be preserved intact when restoring cultural heritage is widely accepted. The concern that filling damaged parts with new material blurs historical authenticity also has merit. However, if one insists on original preservation alone and neglects a crumbling building, the very object to be protected disappears. Authenticity comes not only from preserving old materials but also from openly stating which parts have been restored. Therefore, it is desirable to restore as much as necessary and to record the restored parts distinctly.

A local government finished a housing subsidy pilot program and announced that satisfaction among beneficiary households exceeded 90 percent. The felt sense that the subsidy helped certainly has meaning. But satisfaction only shows the gratitude beneficiaries felt and does not directly measure whether housing stability actually improved. Declaring the program a success without objective indicators such as the number of moves or rent arrears is premature. Whether to expand it can be decided after such indicators are confirmed, and it would not be too late.

The sunset system, which gives regulations a validity period, is evaluated as a device that prevents unnecessary regulations from being left in place. If a regulation disappears automatically on a set date, the department in charge has no choice but to reconsider its necessity. However, if even safety-related regulations are mechanically extinguished, gaps arise and the harm falls on citizens. To realize the purpose of the sunset system, the strictness of extension review should differ according to the nature of the regulation rather than treating all regulations by the same standard.

There is a view that box-office results guarantee a work's value. The fact that many viewers chose it is a signal that cannot be ignored. However, since the number of viewers is also affected by the scale of promotion and the number of screens, it cannot immediately be a measure of artistic quality. Rather, looking at how audiences responded under similar conditions and whether word of mouth lasted over time comes closer to a more accurate evaluation. Therefore, box-office success is only the starting point of evaluation and cannot be the conclusion.

In a survey of 1,000 office workers by a research institute, 68 percent of respondents who had experienced remote work said their job satisfaction had risen. On the other hand, 42 percent said communication among team members had decreased. The institute analyzed that to make the most of the benefits of remote work, communication mechanisms such as regular video meetings are needed.

[Notice] Municipal library facility repair
The municipal library will temporarily close its reading rooms for two weeks, from March 4 to March 17, for facility repair work. During the same period, book loans and returns remain available as usual at the first-floor information desk. We ask for your understanding for the inconvenience caused by construction noise.

Recently, residents' calls to create dog-only zones in downtown parks have been growing. The district office decided to set up two pilot zones within this year and to decide on expansion after checking cases of rule violations and the number of complaints. However, some residents are voicing opposition, citing noise and hygiene problems.

Recently some local governments have been vying to announce how much urban park area they are creating. But park area does not by itself mean a better quality of life for citizens. Even if large green spaces are built on the outskirts where access is poor, residents will find them hard to use in daily life. The success of a policy should be judged not by how much land has been secured but by how many citizens enjoy it close to home. As long as it stays at a numbers race, green-space policy cannot escape the criticism of being administration for show.

This study analyzed the effects of introducing flexible working hours at 320 small and medium-sized firms in the capital region. Employee turnover fell by an average of 3.1 percentage points at firms that adopted the system, but the link with sales growth was not statistically significant. However, because the sample is skewed toward certain industries, there are limits to generalizing the results. Follow-up research therefore needs to re-test the effect across different industries and firm sizes.

The government has decided to expand its budget for responding to the low birth rate in stages from next year. However, this plan differs from earlier ones in that it moves away from cash support and focuses on building up childcare infrastructure. The government judged that childbirth grants alone can hardly resolve the underlying factors that affect the decision to have a child, namely the burden of child-rearing and the difficulty of balancing work and family. Accordingly it plans to put more than half of the budget into expanding daycare centers and after-school care facilities.

The claim that language is not merely a container for thought but a mold that shapes how we think has existed for a long time. This is the so-called linguistic relativity hypothesis. Recent studies tend not to support the hypothesis strongly but accept it in a moderate form: that language may subtly affect the speed at which certain categories are perceived or the direction of attention. In other words, they see language as influencing tendencies of thought rather than determining thought.

After a local hospital announced it would abolish night-time care, protests from residents continued. The hospital cited a shortage of medical staff and deficits. But if night-time care disappears, the first to suffer inconvenience are the elderly, who lack convenient transportation. We cannot wholly deny the hospital's management logic, but we cannot help asking whether it is truly reasonable to judge a highly public service like healthcare by profitability alone. That is why support measures from the local government must go alongside.

The researchers followed 480 elementary school students for two years to examine the relationship between reading volume and vocabulary. The group that read more showed higher vocabulary scores. However, the researchers did not conclude from this that reading raised vocabulary. This is because they cannot rule out the possibility that children who already had strong vocabularies enjoyed reading more from the start. To confirm a causal relationship, they added, experimental research that deliberately varies the reading environment must follow.

Our committee sympathizes with the purpose of this amendment. However, we believe a cautious approach is needed in the way the implementation date is being brought forward. Small workplaces find it hard to secure the staff and money to meet the new standards in a short time, and if standards are tightened without preparation there is a risk that closures will increase contrary to the intent. The committee therefore recommends setting grace periods by size and providing technical support in the meantime.

Workers who flocked to cities in the early industrial period found themselves in poor housing. Intellectuals of the time reacted to this problem in two broad ways. One side pointed to individual moral laxity as the cause and stressed moral reform, while the other sought the cause in structural inequality and demanded institutional improvement. That today's debate over poverty policy resembles this earlier opposition shows how deep the roots of the problem run.

A citizen group demanded that a local council widen the scope of its published minutes. The council had kept some content closed on the grounds that it might invade speakers' privacy. But public statements should be subject to public scrutiny, and hiding even policy discussions unrelated to privacy is weakly persuasive. The scope of information to be protected should be specified concretely, with everything else made public as the rule. A practice of shunning disclosure is the council itself eroding trust.

If this trend continues, regional decline could accelerate.
It is reported that the damage grew because a prompt response was not made.
While the policy's intent is sound, questions remain about the fairness of its enforcement.
The guideline is being criticized for still not being sufficiently observed in the field even after its revision.
Experts predicted that this measure may produce only short-term effects.
The view that this matter should be seen as a structural problem rather than a mere individual deviation is gaining persuasiveness.

A local government announced that retail sales within its area rose 12 percent after it issued more local gift vouchers. But over the same period sales in a neighboring area rose by a similar margin, and more than half of the voucher spending took place at large stores that already had many regular customers. The institute added that this data alone makes it hard to tell whether the vouchers created new consumption or merely changed the payment method for spending that was already planned. The local government said it plans to continue issuing at the same scale next quarter.

The city council passed an ordinance cracking down on delivery motorcycles riding on sidewalks, but decided to delay its enforcement by one year. Council members said there was no disagreement about the need for enforcement. However, it was pointed out that if fines are imposed first without considering the income structure of delivery workers, violations may instead retreat to places where they are less visible. The city explained that it would increase temporary stopping zones during the grace period. The amendment was passed with the approval of most of the members present.

Three other laboratories tried to reproduce the superconducting property of a new material announced by one research team, but two of them failed. The original team countered that a difference in sample purity could be the cause. Even the one laboratory that succeeded said that the measurement temperature range differed, making a direct comparison of the results difficult. The scientific community is neither hastily dismissing this result as an error nor accepting it as an achievement. For this material to become practical, it must first be confirmed whether the same property appears at room temperature.

Merchants say that as the traditional market became known as a tourist spot, visitors increased greatly but regular customers decreased. The market management association assesses that sales rose thanks to foreign visitors. However, some merchants describe today's market as 'the market day is held, but the market has disappeared.' The merchant who said this admitted that daily sales had indeed increased, but trailed off. The association said it plans to expand visitor information centers next year.

The government announced that this year people aged 60 or older made up more than 20 percent of all employed people for the first time ever. However, when the statistics are broken down, most of the increase came from short-term public jobs of under 15 hours a week, and average monthly income actually fell. The criticism that the employment rate as an indicator fails to reflect job quality was repeated this time as well. A government official said a separate analysis by detailed category would be released next month. Experts believe the same figure can lead to different policy diagnoses depending on interpretation.

At a translation conference, a presenter pointed out that the more culturally loaded a word in the source language is, the more the attempt to find and use its closest equivalent flattens the meaning. He acknowledged that the counterargument, that adding footnotes breaks the reader's immersion, has some merit. Even so, he said he wanted to make clear that a translation that is easy to read is not necessarily a translation faithful to the original. The conference decided to make this issue a formal debate topic at next year's meeting.

A public institution said it would release citizens' movement records, with names and addresses removed, to researchers. The institution explained that since all identifying information had been deleted there was no concern about invasion of privacy. However, a legal scholar pointed out that overseas research had reported cases in which specific individuals could be singled out from commuting routes and time slots alone. The institution did not offer a separate position on this point. The release date of the data has not yet been fixed.

A newspaper ran an article titled 'Effect of youth startup grants proven'. But in the body, the one-year survival rate of grant recipients was only 2 percentage points higher than the comparison group, and the researchers also said the sample was small and hard to generalize. In this way the headline carries a stronger assertion than the body's cautious conclusion.

The practice of using question forms in news headlines is growing. There is a defense that it expresses caution in not asserting unconfirmed facts. But a headline like 'Subsidy: will it work?' leaves readers only a negative impression even though the body gives no answer. It amounts to slipping a claim in quietly by borrowing the form of a question. Readers often only skim the headline, so they never get a chance to correct this impression. A question-form headline can be justified only when the body presents grounds for that question.

As the race for breaking news intensifies, unconfirmed information often makes it into headlines. Since readers want quick news, speed itself cannot be blamed. But even if an error is corrected later, the impression left by the first headline is not easily erased, because correction articles are not read as widely as the original. Just because speed and accuracy collide does not mean it should be resolved by shortening the verification stage. Even if late, printing only confirmed facts is the way to keep trust.

The headline 'Bicycle accidents double' grabs readers' attention at once. It is acceptable to say that putting the rate of change first is an efficient way to compress information. But if the baseline count is small, 'double' means little, because the same headline would be possible when one case became two. Conversely, if hundreds of cases doubled, the same headline would carry quite a different weight. When a rate of change is used in a headline, the body must also show the original count so that readers can gauge the scale.

Putting quotation marks in a headline and relaying a statement as it is makes it look like objective delivery without the reporter's subjectivity. Indeed, this method is useful for conveying the statement itself faithfully. But if only the most provocative word is picked from a long statement and put in the headline, quoting becomes selection rather than delivery. Quotation marks may be not a guarantee of accuracy but a trace of editing. Readers should check in the body how the words inside the quotation marks were cut from their context.

News articles follow the inverted-pyramid structure that puts the core in the first paragraph. This structure is efficient in that it lets readers get the gist even if they leave after reading only the beginning. However, the more complex the matter, the more putting only the conclusion in the first paragraph pushes qualifications and counterarguments to the back, so that readers who read only the beginning understand the facts too simply. The very circumstance that many readers do not read to the end becomes the weakness of this structure. It is better to summarize in the first paragraph but include the single most important qualification as well.

A reader who sees the headline 'Consumer prices slow' can easily understand that prices have fallen. One may say it is common knowledge among people who read economic news that this compressed expression means the upward trend has weakened. However, not all readers share that premise, and if only 'slowing' is emphasized while price levels remain high, it can spread an optimism at odds with how people feel. When abbreviating technical terms, one must first consider whether readers hold the same premise.

The word 'controversy' is commonly used in news headlines. It must be acknowledged that it is a convenient word for concisely reporting a matter on which opinions are split. But in practice, 'controversy' is attached even to criticism raised by a few or suspicions with weak grounds, making it look as if society as a whole is divided. A single word inflates the scale of the matter. To use the expression, the body must concretely show who is disputing what.

A newspaper reported, under the headline 'Unemployment surges, a sign of crisis,' that this month's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points from last month to 3.4 percent. However, the announcement of the Employment Trends Institute states that the survey targets sample households and has a statistical error of plus or minus 0.4 percentage points. A change within the margin of error is hard to distinguish as either a real change or a chance result of sampling. Therefore, even if the article body conveys the exact figures, the expression 'surge' in the headline is stronger than the interpretation the figures allow. It is safer to judge after checking the flow over several months rather than one month's fluctuation.

In an opinion poll on a new-town development plan, 48 percent were in favor and 45 percent were opposed, and a broadcaster reported 'Pro-development opinion leads.' The sampling error of this poll is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points at the 95 percent confidence level. Because the 3-point difference between support and opposition lies within the margin of error, one cannot say statistically which side is larger. In such a case, writing 'opinion is evenly split' is an expression more faithful to the data. A report that carries the size of numbers directly over into a ranking is likely to read to readers like a settled fact.

A local paper ran the headline 'Bicycle accidents in the district double.' Looking at the body, the number of accidents rose from 3 last year to 6 this year. In terms of ratio alone it is a 100 percent increase, but because the absolute number is small, even a chance difference of one or two cases changes the ratio greatly. By contrast, car accidents in the same region rose 5 percent, from 1,200 to 1,260, yet did not make the headline. Which side is the risk that readers really need to know about? One should not read the ratio emphasized by the headline as directly indicating the article's importance.

In a bar graph in one article, the average rent of Region A was drawn at more than twice the height of Region B's. But the vertical axis started not at 0 but at 800,000 won. The actual figures are 920,000 won for A and 850,000 won for B, a difference of just over 8 percent. If the starting point is cut off, even a small difference looks like a large gap. Even if the shape of a graph seems to support an article's claim, readers are drawn in by the visual impression unless they check the scale and units.

In weather articles, the expression 'highest temperature since records began' requires care in interpretation. For example, the Onsaemi observatory has recorded temperatures since 1998, so its 'since records began' is merely a ranking within a record of some twenty years. It cannot be placed side by side and compared with the records of other sites that have been observing for nearly a century. Moreover, if the surroundings of the observatory have urbanized and heat accumulates more easily, the causes of the temperature rise include changes in the local environment as well as climate change. Therefore this expression may be true, but that does not directly mean it is direct evidence of climate change.

One article's headline read 'Food additive A raises cancer risk.' But the researcher quoted in the body merely said, 'In mouse experiments there were cases where tumors increased at high doses, so we cannot rule out the possibility of risk to humans as well.' This remark is closer to saying the risk has not yet been ruled out than to saying that the risk has been confirmed. The headline erased the condition 'possibility' and the limitation 'mouse experiment' and left only the conclusion. Quoting a remark does not mean that the caution of that remark was conveyed along with it.

Readers who saw an article titled 'Average salary of office workers: 52 million won' became anxious that their own income fell short of the average. Yet the table of the same survey listed the median as 41 million won. That the average is more than 10 million won above the median means that a small number of high earners pulled the average up. In data whose distribution is skewed to one side, like income, the average may fail to represent the circumstances of ordinary people. The number used in the headline was not wrong, but the anxiety readers felt stems largely from the choice of indicator.
It is risky to judge the whole content of an article from the headline alone.
When citing figures, the surveying body and the survey date must be stated together.

An opinion was raised to skip the safety inspection in order to shorten the construction period. For now it looks like a gain because the schedule is moved up. But once an accident happens, construction actually stops for months and the assigning of blame follows. The proverb 'if you are in a hurry, go the long way around' applies exactly to this case. Rather than rushing and suffering a big loss, following the set procedure turns out to be faster in the end.

In training new employees, the senior staff's explanations always run into the same problem: however thoroughly they explain, it does not sink in for someone who has not seen the site. As the proverb 'hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once' says, seeing a machine run with your own eyes can make hours of explanation understood in minutes. That does not mean explanation is unnecessary. The most effective order is to build a base of understanding through site experience and then organize it through explanation.

Two large delivery platforms competed by cutting fees and vied to advertise benefits for store owners. But once the competition ended, one company acquired the other, and the new operator withdrew the benefits it had promised. Many people say of this, 'When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken.' But this proverb only explains the plight of being hurt in the middle of a fight; it does not cover the situation after the fight ends, where the winner makes the shrimp its new trading partner and changes the terms. The owners' losses should be seen as arising not from being caught up by chance but from a structure designed from the start to make them depend on one side.

People who criticize specialization call a researcher who digs deep into only one field a 'frog in a well.' But water only wells up when the well is deep. The frog's problem is not that it lives in a well but that it cannot imagine a wider sky outside it. A researcher who knows the boundaries of their own field talks with frogs in other wells, brings back new questions, and uses those questions to dig their own well deeper again. So what is needed is not to fill in the wells but to build paths between them.

According to a report by a cultural heritage institute, more than half of the sites found in the last ten years came to light by chance while digging the ground to build new buildings. People have assumed that they already know everything about the ground under the city center simply because it is close. The saying 'It is dark under the lamp' points to a darkness that arises not because things cannot be seen but because no one tries to look. If even a part of the attention poured into distant excavations were turned to what lies underfoot, there would be no small amount of heritage that could be protected before it is damaged.

There is a common belief that if a joint research project has several people in charge, things go wrong. But looking at cases of large-scale research cooperation among several institutions, even with a similar number of participating institutions, some produced results and some did not. What divided them was not the headcount but whether they had set down in writing at the start who held final decision-making power. The boat in the proverb went up the mountain not because many people were rowing but because there was no one to decide the direction. So using 'If there are too many boatmen, the boat goes up the mountain' as grounds for limiting the number of participants is to misidentify the cause.

It is pointed out that most members of a review committee are people who have worked for a long time in the industry under review. The members counter that expertise is needed for a review to be possible. Neither is a wrong statement. However, what the proverb 'The crayfish sides with the crab' points to is not anyone's ill will but the fact that people who have spent time in the same environment look at things by the same standards. Then the solution is neither to tell people to simply trust members' individual conscience nor to exclude everyone from the industry. A realistic approach is to disclose interests and include members from other backgrounds at a set ratio.

The results report of a support project states that the employment rate of participating young people was 85 percent. However, most of the jobs were short-term contracts lasting only during the project period, and even six months after the project ended, the share still remaining at the same workplace was less than one in three. A wild apricot that looks appetizing on the outside can only be known for what it is after you take a bite. To gauge this project's results, one should look at the flesh, the length of retained employment, rather than the skin, the employment rate. Of course, there is no need to deny even the possibility that short-term jobs can be the starting point of a career.

The proverb that childhood habits last a lifetime is often cited as grounds for early education. But neuroscience studies show that the brain can change even after one becomes an adult. That does not mean we can declare the proverb wrong. This is because one can interpret that habits ingrained in childhood last not because they cannot be changed but because they are repeated without any felt need to change them. Read this way, 'A habit from age three lasts until eighty' is closer to a warning that the early environment quietly narrows later choices than to a statement proclaiming destiny.

'Carbon neutrality' means making the amount of greenhouse gas emitted equal to the amount absorbed or removed so that net emissions become zero. This does not mean eliminating emissions completely; it means offsetting the parts that are hard to reduce through forest creation or capture technology. Therefore, achieving carbon neutrality requires both reduction efforts and offsetting means.

A: Some say we should postpone countermeasures because climate model predictions contain error. C: If the numbers differ from model to model, isn't it reasonable to hold off on costly policies until things become more certain? B: It is true that the models differ. B: For postponement to be justified, the uncertainty has to shake even the direction. That is not the case now.

Recently, more people are losing large sums after being taken in by sweet talk promising 'guaranteed principal and 20% monthly returns.' In a normal investment, the greater the return, the greater the risk. A promise of high returns with no risk should be doubted for that very reason. Rather than being drawn in by sweet words and rushing, we need the habit of first checking whether the firm is registered with an official institution.

A food company hid a product defect it knew about, but an internal whistleblower finally brought everything to light. Many people react with relief, saying that justice always prevails. But the fact that the outcome was set right does not mean the process was justified as well. There were already injured consumers, and if the oversight system had been lax the truth might have stayed buried. Justice prevailing does not happen by itself; it becomes possible only when institutions and courage support it.

The saying that the more the better may suit objects, but it is hard to apply to information as it is. With much material, the grounds for judgment seem to grow, but in reality the time and effort needed to sift out what is needed grow too. Moreover, when material of unclear origin is mixed in, the conclusion may actually become blurred. What matters is not how much you have gathered but how accurately you choose and use reliable material.

People who lost their jobs during a recession are often offered comfort with the phrase 'Saeongjima.' It means that the good and bad of life cannot be predicted, so good days will come if you wait. The old man in the tale did not rashly pass judgment on good or bad fortune either when his horse ran away or when it came back. But this phrase does not mean to sit idly and wait for good fortune. Words of comfort cannot replace measures. What the unemployed need is, along with an attitude of calmly accepting uncertainty, concrete support such as retraining and income protection.

When a company put forward a revision plan that kept the total annual salary the same but raised the share of performance bonuses in exchange for lowering base pay, the union objected, calling it 'Josammosa.' The monkeys in the story were foolish because they missed the fact that, whether three in the morning or four, it was seven a day. But this plan has a variable that is not in the monkey story. Bonuses can shrink depending on company results, and base pay is the standard for severance pay and loan screening. Even if the totals look the same, if who bears the risk changes, it is hard to dismiss this as Josammosa.

A local festival succeeded in drawing tourists, and visitors increased every year. But events with resident participation decreased and the stage shifted to center on outside performers. Over this change, the criticism of 'reversal of host and guest' arises. The host of a festival should be the residents who have tended its tradition, yet the guests' tastes have come to decide the content of the event. But one cannot blame the increase in guests itself. The problem is that, on the grounds of welcoming guests, the host has been pushed out of their own place. The success of a festival should be judged not by the number of visitors but by whether residents still stand at the center of the stage.

Many people cite 'Daegi-manseong' against the argument for selecting gifted children early. They say that since there are talents that bloom late, they should not be sorted out early. But this counterargument also has a loophole. Because Daegi-manseong speaks of the result of a great vessel being completed late, it does not tell us about the countless cases that waited to bloom late and never did. Gathering only success stories to discuss the timing of selection is insufficient as grounds. What should be examined instead is whether selection ends with a single round or whether chances are reopened later.

Whenever opinions arise to cut the disaster-response drill budget, the saying 'Yubi-muhwan' is mobilized as the logic of rebuttal. This saying is not wrong but is weak in persuasiveness. When preparation succeeds, nothing happens, so its achievement does not remain as a visible event. The fact that there was no accident can be evidence that the drills were effective, or evidence that drills were unnecessary from the start. So to persuade those in charge of the budget, what is needed is not a slogan but data estimating what damage would have occurred without the drills.

A manufacturer ran a large-scale advertisement promoting eco-friendly management, yet its disclosure documents state that greenhouse gas emissions actually rose in the same period. It is easy to call this 'Pyori-budong.' But Pyori-budong means that the outside and the inside differ, and to say that one must know the inside. If the advertisement explains an emissions reduction plan and the plan is still at the implementation stage, the gap with the current figures may be a time lag rather than deception. The judgment should be made after confirming how specific the reduction plan is and whether it is carried out as promised.

A team that has worked together for a long time is in sync without speaking. People call this 'Isim-jeonsim' and regard it as ideal collaboration. But this approach comes at a cost. Standards shared tacitly are not left in documents, so they vanish all at once when members change. Also, the belief 'we know without saying' even removes the chance to reveal that each understands things differently. Isim-jeonsim shows its strength only on a foundation where important standards have already been put into writing.
